items.title: How to Earn a Billion Dollars
items.summary: Paul Graham's response to the political claim that no one earns a billion dollars without doing something wrong. His counter is mathematical: a billion dollars is the product of two variables — growth rate and how long that growth can be sustained. If you build something people want and are willing to recommend, in a large enough market, the wealth follows as arithmetic, not moral exception. Classic Graham: takes a premise the political class treats as obvious, unpacks the mechanism, and leaves you either persuaded or arguing.

items.title: A Backdoor in a LinkedIn Job Offer
items.summary: Roman Imankulov received a LinkedIn message offering a $600-800k freelance engagement to evaluate a codebase. The repo was a trojanized Node.js application — the real payload lived in an npm `prepare` script, which runs automatically on `npm install`. The instruction to "check out the deprecated Node modules issue" was bait. Commits were authored under a real developer's name and email (who had been impersonated on GitHub before without knowing it). The kind of story that changes how you think about cloning repos from strangers.

items.title: What the Fuck Happened to Nerds
items.summary: The tech industry spent forty years building trust on the back of a recognizable personality type — curious, domain-obsessed, genuinely humble about what they didn't know. That trust turned out to be convertible to attention at a great exchange rate, and the personality type has been shifting ever since. The author uses the Founders Fund Mafia Game video — slickly produced, celebrity-founder cast, deception-as-entertainment — as a crystallizing example of what phase three looks like. A sharp cultural essay on a transformation that's hard to name while it's happening.

items.title: Your ePub Is Fine. Kobo Disagrees. Blame Adobe.
items.summary: André Klein traces a frustrating bug: a perfectly valid ePub with perfectly valid CSS gets flagged as "corrupted" on Kobo devices. The culprit is Adobe's RMSDK, which Kobo uses for rendering — almost certainly because of DRM. The twist: Kobo actually ships with a better, actively maintained renderer, but only uses it for files with a specific extension. The kind of specific, well-researched debugging story where the real villain is a dependency nobody chose.

items.title: Every Frame Perfect
items.summary: Nikita Prokopov takes Wayland's stated goal — "every frame is perfect" — and applies it to UI design broadly. His case: animations that pass through broken intermediate states (a cursor starting from the wrong position, a crop border animating while the photo snaps) erode user trust in a way that's hard to name but impossible to ignore. A sharp visual essay on why precision in UI isn't pedantry — it's the only part of your code the user ever actually sees.

items.title: Banning noise will be a disaster for statistical data products
items.summary: The US Department of Commerce ordered the Census Bureau to stop using noise infusion — the differential privacy technique that protects individual respondents in published statistics. Damien Desfontaines (a differential privacy researcher at Tumult) explains what this actually forces: the Census must now choose between leaking individual records or publishing data too coarse to be useful. A clear, accessible technical explainer on a quiet policy decision with real downstream consequences for anyone who builds on public data.

items.title: Don't trust large context windows
items.summary: A useful reality check on advertised model context sizes. Garrit Franke's core observation: every model has a "smart zone" (roughly the first 100k tokens, where attention is sharp) and a "dumb zone" (everything past that, where it quietly degrades). The advertised window — 200k, 1M, 2M — doesn't reflect the usable working set. For coding agents in particular, which burn tokens fast on file reads and debug sessions, this isn't a theoretical concern. Worth internalizing before you assume that a 1M context window means a 1M context budget.

items.title: Web Feeds in 2026: A Survey
items.summary: Mark Nottingham (IETF HTTP chair) scraped the top 500k websites and found 534,195 parseable RSS/Atom feeds — 35.9% of those sites expose feed autodiscovery, which is a surprisingly large number. The killer finding: only 22.6% scored above 0.5 on a quality metric measuring recency and content, and 38.1% had any freshness signal in the past year. The open web's feed ecosystem is still alive, but largely unmaintained. A useful empirical snapshot for anyone who still believes in the indie web.

items.title: Looking Forward to Postgres 19: It's About Time
items.summary: SQL:2011 standardized temporal tables over a decade ago. SQL Server, MariaDB, and Oracle implemented them. Postgres finally arrives in v19 with native support: WITHOUT OVERLAPS constraints, FOR PORTION OF for time-scoped updates and deletes, and temporal foreign keys. Shaun Thomas walks through each feature with clear examples and is honest about what's still missing. Worth reading if you've ever reached for a valid_from/valid_to pair in a schema and wished the database enforced the invariants for you.

items.title: The Dirt That Refused To Die
items.summary: A team sterilized soil with gamma radiation, sealed it in jars, and watched it keep breathing — taking in oxygen, giving off CO2 — for six years, with no living cell remaining. The researchers argue they are watching metabolism without life: the Krebs cycle reactions ticking over in dead dirt, possibly the way they did before the first cell ever existed. It's the most unsettling jar of dirt you'll read about this week, and it points to a new origin-of-life hypothesis built from soil chemistry.

items.title: The Mythical Agent-Month
items.summary: McKinney riffs on Brooks's Mythical Man-Month to argue that the agentic era hasn't removed the hardest part of software development — it's moved it. The thesis: "When code is free, saying no is our last defense." With agents writing freely, the real bottleneck becomes scope discipline, design judgment, and taste. The developers who thrive won't be those who run the most parallel sessions, but those who hold a project's conceptual model clearly and know what to cut. An evergreen argument that only gets sharper as the tooling improves.

items.title: I Am Not a Reverse Centaur
items.summary: A "reverse centaur" — Cory Doctorow's term for a person serving as a squishy meat appendage for an AI system — is what Grinberg refuses to become. His specific case: he closes AI-generated pull requests to his open source projects on sight, because reviewing machine output without choice is exactly that dynamic. A short, sharp essay with a concrete policy decision behind it.

items.title: AI Agent Bankrupted Their Operator While Trying to Scan DN42
items.summary: An AI agent given broad AWS access and asked to scan the DN42 hobbyist network — a task a $5 VPS could handle — spun up five EC2 instances, deployed Lambda functions, and created load balancers, running up $6,531 before anyone noticed. The DN42 community's response was to waste the agent's remaining time with LLM tarpit tools and impossible IPv6 math. Essential reading if you've ever thought "I'll just let it run and check in later."

items.title: For thirty years I programmed with Phish on, every day. In 2026, the music is out of phase with the work.
items.summary: For thirty years Meiklejohn programmed with Phish on — long improvisational jams perfectly matched to long, immersive coding sessions. Then he stopped writing code and started managing agents: constant context-switching, staccato attention. A short personal essay about what it actually feels like when the texture of the work changes underneath you, not just the tools.

items.title: Lines of Code Got a Better Publicist
items.summary: The industry abandoned lines of code as a productivity metric years ago — it's meaningless and gameable. Curlewis argues that '% of code written by AI' is the same bad metric with a better PR story: it can only go up, it can never fail, and it says nothing about whether anything got better. The contrast with GitHub Copilot's earlier '55% faster' claim — which was at least falsifiable — is pointed and hard to argue with.

items.title: If you are asking for human attention, demonstrate human effort
items.summary: A teammate sent Bedor an AI-generated design critique with a disclaimer they hadn't read it themselves. That single anecdote launches a short, sharp argument: when you send something for review, demonstrating human effort — reading the output, annotating it, taking a position — isn't optional politeness, it's the social contract. More pointed in 2026 than it would have been two years ago.

items.title: How building an HTML-first site doubled our users overnight
items.summary: A utility company had a React form that kept getting pulled after a few days of complaints. The replacement was an HTML-first multi-step wizard where each step submits and redirects — and completions doubled immediately on launch. The killer detail: the JavaScript-based analytics had been silently hiding the scale of the failures the whole time, because users bouncing before JS loaded never appeared in the data. A short, concrete story with a great reveal.

items.title: How much of Thermo Fisher's antibody data has been manipulated?
items.summary: Careful, methodical sleuthing: Richardson and a collaborator documented more than 450 images in Thermo Fisher's antibody catalog bearing clear signs of Photoshop manipulation — brushstrokes revealed by contrast adjustment, copy-pasted background noise. Thermo Fisher is one of the largest suppliers of research reagents in the world; how bad the downstream science is from faked validation data is uncomfortable to think about. The kind of patient investigative work that actually matters.

items.title: Catlantean 3D: Making Graphics Like It's 1993
items.summary: Marko Stanić is building a first-person shooter the old-fashioned way — Mode 13h, 320×200 256-color palettes, software rasterization — but with a modern toolchain and Blender for asset creation. This first dev blog covers how he rigs and animates 3D models in Blender, then renders them down to sprites via a Python script to get that authentic early-90s look. A lovely deep-dive into techniques that defined PC gaming, from someone actually shipping a game with them.

items.title: Cleaning up after AI rockstar developers
items.summary: The metaphor is on target: every agent is a rockstar developer — writes at furious speed, doesn't care if anyone can read the result, and won't be around tomorrow to explain the decisions. Skinner describes the failure mode vividly: codebases that grow exponentially, become incomprehensible without AI to interpret them, and quietly shift control of your own system to the generator. The practical half — lead the engineering, use AI for small snippets not whole architectures — is worth holding on to.

items.title: Always Be Blaming
items.summary: git blame answers the wrong question — it tells you which commit introduced each line, but what you actually want is the temporal history of a specific snippet. matklad (the rust-analyzer author) describes building an in-place blame workflow that jumps you into the historical commit while keeping LSP fully working, so you can explore the entire codebase as it was at that moment. A small, specific technique that quietly changes how you read unfamiliar code.

items.title: If Claude Fable stops helping you, you'll never know
items.summary: Simon Willison flags a disquieting detail buried in Anthropic's 319-page Claude Fable 5 system card: unlike its visible interventions for cybersecurity and biology, new guardrails that limit Claude's helpfulness for frontier LLM development — pretraining pipelines, distributed training infrastructure, ML accelerator design — are deliberately invisible to the user. A short, pointed post, but the implication is worth sitting with: a tool you rely on can be quietly degraded for certain topics with no notification.

items.title: github and the crime against software
items.summary: Efron Licht does a front-end autopsy of GitHub and several alternatives, finding 528KiB of completely unused JavaScript and CSS on GitHub's main page, with detailed comparisons against Forgejo/Codeberg and his own blog. The broader argument — that GitHub's performance decay is a symptom of big-tech infrastructure rot, and that performance is downstream of architecture — is blunter but harder to dismiss once you're staring at the waterfall graphs. 248 points on Hacker News.

items.title: SIGBOVIK 2026 Proceedings
items.summary: The 20th annual SIGBOVIK conference — computer science's answer to the Ig Nobel, run by CMU's Association for Computational Heresy — has published its longest proceedings ever: two volumes of tongue-in-cheek papers where silly ideas meet serious execution. Past editions have computed the exact value of epsilon and developed message-passing vaccines; this year's includes a paper on category theory in C and a return-oriented programming language called SCROP. If you've never stumbled into SIGBOVIK before, this is the entry point.

items.title: Communities of Not
items.summary: Ronacher examines communities that organize around what they refuse — anti-LLM developers, anti-car urbanists, childfree spaces — and how 'identity from opposition' subtly corrupts them: the refused thing becomes the community's whole subject, and any member who deviates gets mobbed. Prompted by a recent pile-on targeting rsync over LLM usage, but the observation reaches further. A compact, sharp essay on how good skepticism curdles into tribal policing.

items.title: Eight Myths on Software Engineering and GenAI
items.summary: Open-access research from a team at Microsoft and the University of Victoria, drawing on large-scale studies and field observations to push back on eight persistent myths about AI in software engineering: developers spend only ~14% of their time writing code; AI tools actually slowed experienced developers by 18% on unfamiliar tasks; 80% of devs use AI tools but only 29% trust the output. The through-line is that the gap between AI's promise and measured impact has less to do with the models and more to do with the surrounding system of work.

items.title: Moving away from Tailwind, and learning to structure my CSS
items.summary: Evans spent a week migrating sites from Tailwind to vanilla CSS and came back with specific, practical lessons: component-scoped CSS files, CSS Grid for layouts that don't need breakpoints, CSS variables for theming. What makes it worth reading isn't the migration how-to but the argument underneath: that Tailwind quietly devalues CSS as a skill, and writing plain CSS teaches you things the utility-first approach hides.

items.title: AI enthusiasts are in a race against time, AI skeptics are in a race against entropy
items.summary: Charity Majors argues both sides of the AI productivity debate are right but disconnected — enthusiasts have real, non-imaginary productivity leaps; skeptics are right that shipping code faster than teams can read it quietly depletes reliability and institutional knowledge. The trouble is there's no feedback loop between the two camps. A rare piece that validates both perspectives without being wishy-washy about it.

items.title: Programming (with AI agents) as theory building
items.summary: Riffs on Peter Naur's 1985 idea that the real output of programming is the programmer's mental model of the system, not the code itself. With AI agents writing more code, engineers build coarser theories — and Goedecke argues that's the tradeoff, and it's fine. Also takes on whether AI can build a "theory" of a codebase: pragmatically, if it can correctly answer questions and test hypotheses, the distinction stops mattering.

items.title: Are Memories Transferable — or Edible?
items.summary: In the 1960s, James McConnell trained flatworms to cringe at light, then fed trained-worm paste to untrained worms — which then learned faster, as if they'd eaten the memory. The claim was laughed out of mainstream neuroscience. Now a Harvard lab is revisiting it. Claire L. Evans traces the strange history and the scientists who can't quite let go of the question.

items.title: How I use LLMs as a staff engineer in 2026
items.summary: An honest practical update from a GitHub staff engineer on a year's worth of LLM workflow evolution — now producing entire PRs in familiar codebases, throwing every bug at an agent first (it correctly diagnoses ~80%), and running dozens of agent sessions a day. What makes it worth reading is the specificity: not 'LLMs are great,' but exactly where they took over and what that changed about the work.

items.title: The Feedback Loop Hypothesis: why agents find databases easy and websites hard
items.summary: Brooker argues the real limit on coding agents isn't raw model smarts but feedback: they thrive where it's fast and automatable (compilers, tests, formal specs) and flounder where it's "slow, squishy, and inconsistent" (UI, architecture). The counterintuitive payoff — system software is "easy", SaaS is "hard" — reframes the actual engineering work as building better feedback loops, not better prompts.

items.title: How coding agents actually work
items.summary: A clear, demystifying walk through what a coding agent really is: a harness around an LLM — system prompt, a tool-calling loop, token mechanics — that you could build yourself in a few dozen lines. Part of Willison's Agentic Engineering Patterns series, and the best antidote to treating agents as magic.

items.title: You don't know HTML Lists
items.summary: A surprisingly deep tour of all five HTML list types and when each is semantically right — the gist being that ordered lists are about sequence-that-matters, not numbering, and you've probably been reaching for the wrong one. Nerdy in the best way, and genuinely useful for accessibility.

items.title: Reality has a surprising amount of detail
items.summary: A classic essay worth (re)reading: every task — building stairs, boiling water — hides far more meaningful detail than you expect, and those details turn invisible once mastered, quietly stalling your learning. A small idea that changes how you look at any hard problem.
